sources.entry: concurrent.futures - (Python standard library) High-level asynchronous execution of callables.

summary.name: concurrent.futures
summary.one_liner: Python standard library module providing a high-level interface for running callables asynchronously in thread, interpreter, or process pools.
use_cases: running I/O-bound tasks such as fetching URLs concurrently
running isolated tasks across multiple interpreters
copying or processing many files concurrently
collecting results of background jobs as they finish
summary.what_it_does: ["Provides an abstract Executor interface with submit() and map() for scheduling callables asynchronously.", "ThreadPoolExecutor runs calls in a pool of threads, with a default worker count based on CPU count.", "ProcessPoolExecutor runs calls in separate processes via multiprocessing, sidestepping the GIL but requiring picklable functions and arguments.", "InterpreterPoolExecutor (added in 3.14) runs each worker in its own isolated interpreter for multi-core parallelism, with data passed by pickling.", "Future objects offer result(), exception(), cancel(), done() and add_done_callback(); wait() and as_completed() help coordinate many futures."]
notable: Same Executor interface across thread, interpreter, and process pools
ProcessPoolExecutor on Windows limits max_workers to 61
Documented deadlock pitfalls when a future waits on another future in the same single-worker pool
caveats: Not available on WASI or WebAssembly platforms
ProcessPoolExecutor cannot be used from the interactive interpreter and requires picklable callables
ThreadPoolExecutor threads are joined before interpreter exit, so it is not recommended for long-running tasks
